blocks.text: Pick the Tool by Where the Change Lives
Undoing in Git depends on two questions: which area the change is in (working tree, index, or a commit), and whether the commit has already been shared with others.

rows: Discard unstaged edits to a file
Unstage a file but keep the edits
Restore a file as it was in an older commit
Fix the last commit's message or add a forgotten file
Undo local commits, keep changes staged
Undo local commits, keep changes unstaged
Throw away local commits and all changes
Undo a commit that is already pushed

blocks.text: git restore (Git 2.23+) replaces the file-restoring half of the overloaded git checkout. By default it restores the working tree from the index; --staged restores the index from HEAD; --source picks any commit.

$ git restore src/api.py                 # discard unstaged edits
$ git restore --staged src/api.py        # unstage, keep edits
$ git restore --staged --worktree src/api.py   # both: back to HEAD
$ git restore --source=v1.2.0 config.yml # take the file from a tag

$ git commit -m "Add stock endpont"
$ git add tests/test_stock.py            # forgot the test
$ git commit --amend -m "Add stock endpoint"

# Keep the message, just add staged changes
$ git commit --amend --no-edit

Amend does not modify a commit; commits are immutable. It creates a new commit with a new ID and moves the branch to it. If the old commit was already pushed, your branch and the remote now diverge and you would need a force push. Only amend commits you have not shared.
git reset: Moving the Branch Pointer
git reset <commit> moves the current branch to another commit. The mode decides what happens to the index and the working tree.

rows: Squash the last few commits into one: reset --soft, then commit
Discard everything and return to a known state

# Combine the last 3 local commits into one
$ git reset --soft HEAD~3
$ git commit -m "Add stock endpoint with tests"
git revert: Undoing Shared History Safely
git revert creates a new commit whose changes are the inverse of an existing commit. History is only appended to, never rewritten, so it is safe on branches other people have pulled, including main.

$ git revert 4b8d0a1
[main 8e2f1d0] Revert "Fix CORS config"

# Revert a range without committing each one, then commit once
$ git revert --no-commit HEAD~3..HEAD
$ git commit -m "Revert stock feature"

Reverting a merge commit requires telling Git which parent is the main line: git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>. It also has a subtle consequence when you later try to re-merge the same branch. Module 4 covers this in detail.
Rewrite history freely while it is private; once it is shared, add to it instead of rewriting it.

git reset --hard and git restore on unstaged edits destroy work that was never committed, and the reflog cannot bring it back because the reflog only tracks commits. Content that had been staged may still be recoverable as dangling blobs with git fsck --lost-found, but do not rely on it. When in doubt, commit or stash first.

Legacy equivalents you will see in older docs and answers: git checkout -- <file> equals git restore <file>, and git reset HEAD <file> equals git restore --staged <file>. Prefer the newer commands; they have one clear job each.
